title: Parvati's tapas
hookLine: Parvati wins Shiva by her own tapas, and refuses to hear him mocked; why Hindus still keep vows and fasts for Shiva
carry: tapas: devotion proven by steady effort
tomorrow: why did Parvati's mother faint at the wedding?

lines: A VISITOR COMES UP THE PATH.
cards: A princess takes off her jewels. She sets aside her silk and puts on bark. She leaves her father's palace for the mountains, a place where Shiva once sat, and begins.
In the Shiva Purana, Parvati has seen what happened to Kama. Beauty didn't win Shiva; help from the gods didn't win him. So she'll do what Shiva himself does.

She'll practice tapas. And one day, deep into it, a visitor comes up the path: a young ascetic with matted hair and a staff, who sits down and asks, very politely, what on earth she thinks she's doing.

teach.b: Tapas is austerity, disciplined effort that burns away what's easy and leaves what's strong. In the story, Parvati's tapas grows harder and harder. She stands in the cold, and sits among fires in the heat.
She eats less, then less again, and tradition says she gave up even fallen leaves, which is why one of her names is Aparna. Then the visitor. He's courteous at first, then starts in on Shiva.
Why this one? He smears himself with ash from cremation grounds. He wears snakes and rides a bull.
No house, no family, and he burned the god of love. A woman like you, he says, could marry anyone. Parvati's answer is the heart of the selection.
She doesn't argue with the facts.

She says, in effect, that the visitor doesn't know who Shiva is: what looks poor and strange from outside is exactly what she loves. And she won't sit and listen to him being insulted. She gets up to leave.
Then the visitor drops the disguise. It's Shiva himself, who came to test her and found her immovable. Where Kama's arrow failed, her own tapas succeeds.
Shiva agrees to marry her. Here is the teaching. Tapas isn't punishing yourself.
In Hindu practice it's devotion you can see: steady effort offered to God, kept up when it's hard and when someone calls it pointless.
That's why so many Hindus keep a vrata, a vow, for Shiva: a Monday fast, or the Teej fast women keep in memory of Parvati's. Small tapas, offered for love.

how: Hindus tell Parvati's tapas and her marriage to Shiva in the Shiva Purana and in poetry; many devotees keep Monday fasts for Shiva, and some women keep fasts in Parvati's honor, such as Hartalika Teej, praying for a good marriage or for their husbands' welfare.

games.q: you're Parvati, deep in tapas. a polite young ascetic lists everything wrong with Shiva and says you could marry anyone. what do you do?
o: argue point by point that Shiva isn't so strange.
refuse to listen and get up to leave.
games.why: she won't hear Shiva insulted and gets up to go. then the visitor drops the disguise: it was Shiva, testing her.

practice: Pick one small vow you'll keep steady this week, the way families keep a Monday fast for Shiva: a lamp each evening, a few rounds of Om Namah Shivaya. If you don't pray, choose one steady practice of attention instead.
When a voice starts in, telling you it's pointless, notice it the way Parvati noticed the visitor, and stay put.
